result:
I tested 8 properties of `eml_parser.parser` and found 3 real bugs. All three reproduce with the inputs below, and I wrote a bug report file for each.

| # | Bug | Severity | Report |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `ignore_bad_start=True` corrupts every message. Even on a clean email, `from` comes back as `'alice@example.comto'`, and To and Subject come back empty. | High (Logic) | `bug_report_eml_parser_parser_2026-10-28_19-27_ku2z.md` |
| 2 | Every attachment without a filename is reported as `part-000`, because the counter is never advanced between sibling parts. | Low (Logic) | `bug_report_eml_parser_parser_2026-10-28_19-27_7721.md` |
| 3 | `email_regex` takes quadratic time on Received headers, which aren't split into chunks the way bodies are. A 100 KB header of `a`s takes about 10.6 s; extrapolating, 1 MB would take about 17 minutes. This is a denial-of-service risk for a tool that parses untrusted email. | Medium | `bug_report_eml_parser_parser_2026-10-28_19-27_gjbm.md` |

**Causes and fixes:**
- **Bug 1** has two separate mistakes:
  - `b':' not in eml_file.split(b'\n', 1)` tests whether `b':'` is an item in the list, not whether it appears in the first line, so the skipping code almost always runs.
  - That code then joins the lines back together without the `\n` between them.
- **Bug 3:** I timed each regex on its own, and `email_regex` is the only one that slows down this way. Capping the part before the `@` at 64 characters (`{1,64}`, the RFC 5321 maximum) cuts 100 KB to 14 ms. It returned the same matches as the original on 200k random short strings.
- I applied the fixes for bugs 1 and 2 outside the library code and they gave the right output: `part-000, part-001`, and the correct from/to/subject. The library files themselves are unchanged.

**Passed (5):**
- Splitting a long body into chunks never loses text.
- A short URL anywhere in a long body is extracted whole.
- IP addresses are returned in standard form, both on their own and after an `@`.
- The To header comes back as a lower-cased address list.
- Random header and body bytes don't cause a crash.

I didn't hand-build an input that should fail to confirm each passing test could actually fail, so treat those passes as moderately strong evidence.

Files are in `runs/eml-parser_v2_r2/`:
- `claims.md`
- `test_parser_props.py`
- the three bug reports
